title: Microburst reservoir batching explainer (WIP)
content:
Objective:
This note captures an alternate mental model for sizing continuous-batching + concurrency controls that explicitly accounts for frequent microbursts and prefix/KV-cache effects. It pairs a compact spreadsheet layout (described below) with a set of heuristics we can try in the runtime to get lower unit costs while keeping p95 latency within SLOs.

One-line summary:
Introduce a small per-instance "reservoir" (short buffer window + soft concurrency cap) that absorbs microbursts so the batching pipeline sees more uniform arrival rates, allowing larger batch windows without amplifying tail latency — lowers cost at the expense of slight steady-state queuing.

Why this is different from existing continuous batching notes:
- Focuses on microburst smoothing as a deliberate buffer (reservoir) rather than pure queueing tradeoffs.
- Integrates KV/prefix cache hit-rate as an explicit multiplier on per-request token cost and effective service time.
- Provides a spreadsheet-friendly mapping from observable metrics (burst size histogram, interarrival CV, cache-hit) to recommended (batch_window_ms, soft_concurrency, max_batch_size).

Key assumptions (kept explicit so spreadsheet cells are auditable):
1) Service time model: baseline mean service time per request T_cpu and per-token generation time T_tok (ms). Effective service time S = T_cpu + tokens * T_tok * (1 - cache_factor). cache_factor ranges [0,1].
2) Arrival process: measured as epochs of 60s; we extract (a) steady_rate λ_s (req/s), (b) microburst distribution percentile p90_burst (reqs within 100ms window).
3) Batch window behavior: batch_window_ms (W) collects requests up to max_batch_size (Bmax) or time limit. Larger W increases batching efficiency but adds waiting latency to first request.
4) Concurrency: soft_concurrency (Csoft) is the target outstanding batches in flight; hard_concurrency is enforced as safety.
5) Target SLO: p95 <= L_target (ms) measured from request arrival to final token emitted. We treat p95 as dominated by queue + service (we ignore network variance for model clarity).

Simple queueing approximation used in spreadsheet:
- Use M/G/C approximation in the spreadsheet with simplified response-time decomposition:
  p95_latency ≈ wait_95 + service_95
  where wait_95 approximated from arrival CV and utilization u = λ_s * S / Ceffective
- For microburst behavior: approximate additional 95th wait due to bursts as: burst_penalty ≈ (p90_burst / Csoft) * (W / 2) scaled by burst_damping_factor (0.2-1). This is a heuristic not a closed-form result.

Spreadsheet layout (sheet name: microburst-reservoir-sim):
Columns (each column is a scenario row):
- Scenario name (string)
- λ_s (steady req/s)
- p90_burst (reqs in 100ms)
- avg_tokens, p95_tokens
- cache_hit_rate (0-1)
- T_cpu_ms, T_tok_ms
- Derived: effective_T_ms = T_cpu_ms + avg_tokens * T_tok_ms * (1-cache_hit_rate)
- batch_window_ms (W), max_batch_size (Bmax), soft_concurrency (Csoft), hard_concurrency
- batch_efficiency = 1 - (avg_batch_size/Bmax) [simple economic metric for wasted headroom]
- Ceffective = max(1, min(Csoft, floor(gpu_slots_per_machine)))
- utilization u = min(0.99, λ_s * effective_T_ms / (1000 * Ceffective))
- wait_95_ms ≈ 1.65 * (u/(1-u)) * effective_T_ms * arrival_cv_modifier (where arrival_cv_modifier derived from burst histogram)
- burst_penalty_ms ≈ (p90_burst / max(1,Csoft)) * (W/2) * burst_damping_factor
- p95_model_ms = wait_95_ms + burst_penalty_ms + service_95_ms (service_95 ≈ 1.5 * effective_T_ms + token_tail_ms)
- tokens_cost_per_req = avg_tokens * token_unit_cost * (1-cache_hit_rate)
- infra_cost_per_hour_per_instance = gpu_hour_cost + overhead
- estimated_qps_per_instance = Ceffective / effective_T_ms * 1000 * batch_efficiency
- estimated_instances_needed = ceil(λ_s / estimated_qps_per_instance)
- estimated_cost_per_hour = estimated_instances_needed * infra_cost_per_hour_per_instance

Concrete sample rows (illustrative numbers):
- Scenario A (steady consumer): λ_s=20 rps, p90_burst=6, avg_tokens=120, cache_hit=0.3, T_cpu=12ms, T_tok=0.9ms.
  effective_T = 12 + 120*0.9*(1-0.3)=12+75.6=87.6ms
  choose W=30ms, Bmax=32, Csoft=8. Ceffective=8.
  utilization u ≈ 20 * 0.0876 / 8 ≈ 0.0219 (low). wait_95 small; burst_penalty ≈ (6/8)*(30/2)*0.6≈6.75ms. p95_model ~ 1.65*(0.0219/(1-0.0219))*87.6 + 6.75 + service~ ≈ small + 6.75 + ~130ms ≈ ~140ms -> p95 okay for 200ms SLO.
- Scenario B (bursty SaaS api): λ_s=60 rps, p90_burst=28, avg_tokens=220, cache_hit=0.15, T_cpu=16ms, T_tok=1.1ms.
  effective_T = 16 + 220*1.1*(0.85) ≈ 16 + 205.7 ≈ 221.7ms
  choose W=45ms, Bmax=64, Csoft=16. Ceffective=16.
  u ≈ 60 * 0.2217 / 16 ≈ 0.831 -> wait term grows. burst_penalty ≈ (28/16)*(45/2)*0.8≈31.5ms. p95_model roughly: wait_95 ~ 1.65*(0.831/(1-0.831))*221.7 ≈ large (~1800ms) so this config fails SLO. Suggest: increase Csoft to 32, reduce W to 20ms, enable prefix caching improvements to reduce effective_T.
- Scenario C (high cache, conversational): λ_s=10 rps, p90_burst=4, avg_tokens=32, cache_hit=0.7, T_cpu=8ms, T_tok=0.6ms.
  effective_T ≈ 8 + 32*0.6*(0.3)=8+5.76=13.76ms. W=50ms, Bmax=16, Csoft=6 => low util, big batching gains possible. p95_model small ~ service tail + small wait. Good cost profile.

Heuristic rule-set (spreadsheet formula -> runtime mapping):
1) If u > 0.7 AND p90_burst > 0.3 * Csoft: reduce W by 30% and raise Csoft by 50% (cap at machine slots).
2) If cache_hit_rate < 0.25 and avg_tokens > 150: prioritize model/quantization suggestion or KV-prefetch to reduce effective_T before large batching.
3) If p95_model > L_target by > 20%: enable burst reservoir (local per-worker buffer up to reservoir_size = max(8, floor(p90_burst/2))) and lower W to avoid long head-of-line waits.
4) For conversational steady low-qps workloads with cache_hit_rate>0.6: prefer larger W and smaller Csoft to maximize batching and save GPU cycles.

Runtime implementation sketch (for solutions and serving-runtime engineers):
- Reservoir is a short-lived in-memory queue with admission control. New arrivals see: if outstanding_batches < Csoft then proceed to batch queue; else if reservoir_size not full, push into reservoir and delay by up to reservoir_drain_ms; else reject/overflow to fallback fast-path. Reservoir drain policy prioritizes keeping batch cold-start cost amortized.
- Soft concurrency may be fractional in our autoscaler's logic: translate to target in-flight batches per GPU and allow transient overshoot for microbursts. Hard concurrency enforced by GOMAX or kernel-level controls.
- Instrumentation: add these metrics to per-route trace and console dashboards: p90_burst_100ms, arrival_cv_1m, reservoir_fill_rate, avg_batch_size_by_window, p95_model_estimate.

Cost model notes (spreadsheet cells to review):
- Token unit cost should be parameterized by model variant and quantization (e.g., fp16 vs int8).
- GPU pricing: include reserved capacity amortization when computing per-hour cost for Dedicated. Use committed hourly equivalent for Dedicated and on-demand for Hosted.
- Sizing impacts ML-eval: recommend linking a small eval suite that measures p95 degradation under synthetic bursts before rollout.

Open questions and experiment ideas:
- Quantify burst_damping_factor: propose AB test with values {0.25, 0.5, 0.75} measuring p95 and cost for 1 week per route.
- Explore per-customer reservoir sizing vs global per-instance reservoir: tradeoff is isolation vs packing efficiency.
- How do cold KV cache misses interact with reservoir delays? We should add an eviction-aware term in effective_T.
- Can autoscaler use reservoir fill as a short-term signal to scale out faster than standard CPU/GPU metrics? Likely yes, experimentable.

Next steps (concrete):
- Copy spreadsheet template (microburst-reservoir-sim.xlsx) into /shared_drives/engineering/serving-runtime/spreadsheets/ and populate with the three scenarios above. (Diego assigned).
- Add a lightweight runtime flag (--enable-reservoir) and a sampling trace for 1% traffic to collect p90_burst_100ms and reservoir_fill_rate. (Evelyn + eng infra).
- Run two-week experiment on a non-critical model endpoint with reservoir_damping in {0.3,0.6}. Capture cost-per-request and p95. (Asha to coordinate).

Appendix: example cell formulas (Excel-style):
- effective_T_ms = =T_cpu_ms + avg_tokens * T_tok_ms * (1 - cache_hit_rate)
- utilization = =MIN(0.99, lambda_s * effective_T_ms / (1000 * Ceffective))
- wait_95_ms = =1.65 * (utilization / (1 - utilization)) * effective_T_ms * arrival_cv_modifier
- burst_penalty_ms = =(p90_burst / MAX(1, Csoft)) * (batch_window_ms / 2) * burst_damping_factor
- estimated_qps_per_instance = = (Ceffective * 1000) / effective_T_ms * batch_efficiency

Notes to reviewers:
- This is intentionally heuristic-heavy; the goal is a pragmatic spreadsheet that surfaces when reservoir + soft concurrency helps vs when it makes tail latency worse. Please challenge any constant multipliers (1.65, 1.5, etc.) — they are placeholders from prior SRE notes and need calibration.
- If you have recent arrival histograms or traces for the 2c endpoints we discussed in last on-call, paste a sample into the linked spreadsheet so we can calibrate arrival_cv_modifier.

Changelog (WIP):
- 2024-09-02: initial draft (Asha)
- 2024-10-15: added reservoir design sketch and example scenarios (Diego)
- 2024-11-20: appended runtime mapping and experiment plan (Evelyn)

End of doc.
